en: The Gorakṣa-śataka:
Oṃ. Commencement of the Gorakṣa-śataka on Haṭha-yoga.
I bow to the venerable Guru, supreme bliss, whose form is self-bliss.
By the mere presence of whom the body becomes filled with consciousness and bliss. (Gorakṣaśataka 2.1)

I incessantly worship the illustrious Mīnanātha, who is superior to both the manifest and the unmanifest qualities; he in whom the Primordial Lord himself became an ocean of the fragrance of knowledge, and by whom you are celebrated as one who has mastered the calculation of time through ages and kalpas by means of binding his own support and the like, with the flame of his inner lamp unwavering. (Gorakṣaśataka 2)
Having bowed with devotion to his guru, Gorakṣa speaks this supreme knowledge, which is desired by yogins and brings about the highest bliss. (Gorakṣaśataka 3)
Gorakṣa speaks this hundred [of verses] out of a desire for the welfare of yogins;
by the certain realization of which the supreme state arises. (GorS 2.4)
This is the ladder to liberation, this is the deception of time:
that the mind, having turned away from delusion, is attached to the Supreme Self. (GorS 2.5 = 1.2)

The virtuous person practices yoga, which is the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree of the Vedas— whose branches are frequented by the twice-born— and which brings about the pacification of the suffering of worldly existence.
Posture, restraint of breath, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption—these are the six limbs of yoga. (Gorakṣaśataka 2.7 = 1.4)
There are as many seats as there are species of living beings;
Maheśvara knows all their various distinctions. (GorS 2.8 = 1.5)
Each one of the eighty-four lakhs has been proclaimed;
from that, Śiva made one hundred and sixteen sacred seats (pīṭhas). (GorS 2.9 = 1.6)
Among all seats, only two are distinguished:
one is declared to be Siddhāsana, and the second is Kamalāsana. (Gorakṣaśataka 2.10 = 1.7)

Having firmly placed the root of one foot upon the perineum (yoni-sthānaka), and having made the body perfectly balanced and motionless, with the senses restrained and the gaze fixed between the eyebrows—this, which causes the breaking open of the door to liberation, is called Siddhāsana. (Gorakṣaśataka 2.11 = 1.8)

Having placed the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left foot upon the right thigh, holding them firmly with both hands according to the prescribed method, and placing the two big toes at the heart, one should gaze at the tip of the nose; this is called the lotus posture (padmāsana), which removes the afflictions of disease for those who practice self-restraint. (Gorakṣaśataka 12 = 1/9)
How can those yogins achieve perfection who do not know within their own bodies the six cakras, the sixteen supports, the three lakṣas, and the five voids? (Gorakṣaśataka 13)
How can those who do not know their own body to be a house with one pillar, nine doors, and five presiding deities become accomplished yogins? (Gorakṣaśataka 14)
The *ādhāra* should have four petals, and the *svādhiṣṭhāna* has six petals;
there is a ten-petaled lotus at the navel, and one with petals numbering twelve in the heart.
There should be a sixteen-petaled [lotus] at the throat, and likewise a two-petaled one between the eyebrows;
that which is called the thousand-petaled [lotus] is said to be at the Brahma-aperture on the Great Path.
The Foundation is the first wheel, and the Self-Abiding is the second;
situated between the two, the Place of the Yoni is called Kāmarūpa. (GorS 2.17 = 1.10)
The region of the anus, known as the Foundation (Ādhāra), is a four-petalled lotus;
in its center is said to be the Yoni, Kāmākṣā, who is worshipped by the Siddhas. (GorS 2.18 = 1.11)
He who knows that the great liṅga stands facing west within the womb, its form like a jewel upon the head, is a knower of yoga. (GorS 2.19 = 1.12)
Resembling molten gold and flashing like a streak of lightning, that triangular city of Fire is established below the genitals. (GorS 20 = 1/13)
When that supreme light, infinite and facing in all directions, is perceived within that great yoga, the coming and going [of rebirth] no longer exists. (Gorakṣaśataka 21)
By its own name, it is *prāṇa*; its support is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
From this station, the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, the penis itself is designated [as the *meḍhra*]. (GorS 2.22 = 1.14)
Where the *kanda* is strung like a jewel upon a thread by means of the *suṣumṇā*, that navel-center is called the *maṇipūraka-cakra*. (Gorakṣaśataka 23 = 1/15)
In the great wheel with twelve spokes, which is devoid of merit and demerit, the individual soul wanders as long as it does not find the ultimate reality. (Gorakhśataka 24)
Above the penis and below the navel is the source of the *kanda*, like the egg of a bird;
there, seventy-two thousand channels have arisen. (GorS 25 = 1/16)
Among those thousands of channels, seventy-two are declared to be the principal carriers of the vital breath (prāṇa); furthermore, ten among them are traditionally recognized as the most important.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā as the third;
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśasvinī. (GorS 2.27 = 1.18)
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth;
this wheel consisting of channels (nāḍī-cakra) should always be known by yogins. (GorS 28 = 1/19)
The *iḍā* is situated on the left side, and likewise the *piṅgalā* on the right;
the *suṣumṇā* is in the middle region, while the *gāndhārī* is in the left eye. (GorS 29 = 1/20)
On the right [side] is Hastijihvā, and Pūṣā is on the right ear;
Yaśasvinī is on the left ear, and Alambuṣā is also on the seat.
Kuhū is in the region of the genitals, and Śaṅkhinī is at the root-base;
thus, ten channels remain stationed, having taken recourse to the gateway. (GorS 2.31 = 1.22)
The three channels known as iḍā, piṅgalā,
and suṣumṇā are declared to be the constant carriers of the vital breath (prāṇa), having the moon, the sun, and fire as their presiding deities.
The vital airs are Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna;
as well as Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.
The prāṇa always dwells in the heart; the apāna is in the region of the anus;
the samāna should be in the region of the navel; and the udāna resides in the middle of the throat. (Gorakṣa Śataka 34)
The one called Nāga is known for belching; Kūrma is remembered for opening the eyes;
Kṛkara should be understood as that which causes sneezing; and Devadatta is present during yawning. (Gorakṣa Śataka 35)
Even when one has died, it does not abandon [the body], for it is all-pervading, O Dhanañjaya;
these, in the form of the individual soul (jīva), wander through all the channels (nāḍīs). (Gorakṣaśataka 36 = 1/25)
Just as a ball, when struck by a staff-like arm, flies upward, so too the living soul, impelled by the prāṇa and apāna breaths, does not remain still. (GorS 2.38 = 1.27)
The living soul, under the sway of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, indeed runs upward and downward;
because of its restlessness on the left and right paths, it is not perceived. (GorS 2.39 = 1.26)
Just as a hawk bound by a string is pulled back even though it has flown away, so the individual soul (jīva), bound by the qualities (guṇas), is drawn along by the out-breath and in-breath. 40 (1/28)
The apāna draws up the prāṇa, and the prāṇa draws up the apāna;
the knower of yoga unites these two as they are situated above and below. (Gorakṣaśataka 41 = 1/29)
With the syllable *ha* it goes out, and with the syllable *sa* it enters again;
the individual soul (*jīva*) constantly recites this mantra, "haṃsa, haṃsa. (GorS 2.42)
Twenty-one thousand six hundred times;
endowed with this number, the living being constantly recites the mantra. (GorS 2.43)
The Gāyatrī known as Ajapā bestows liberation upon yogins;
by the mere intention of this [mantra], one is released from all sins. (GorS 2.44)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a knowledge like this, a recitation like this, or a wisdom like this.
Gāyatrī, the sustainer of life-force (prāṇa), has arisen from Kuṇḍalinī;
he who knows that great science of life-force (prāṇavidyā) is a knower of Yoga. (Gorakṣaśataka 46)
Above the *kanda*, the Kuṇḍalinī power, coiled eightfold, remains eternally covering the opening of the door of Brahman with her mouth. (GorS 2.47 = 1.30)
Having covered with her mouth that door through which one must go to the stainless abode of Brahman, the Supreme Goddess lies fast asleep. (Gorakṣaśataka 48)
Awakened by the yoga of fire and struck by the mind, it seizes the thread like a needle and ascends through the *suṣumṇā*. (GorS 2.49 = 1.31)
Resembling a quivering serpent, beautiful like a lotus fiber,
once awakened by the application of fire, it ascends through the *suṣumṇā* for the sake of the vow.
Just as one might forcibly open a door-panel with a key, so too the yogi should pierce the gate of liberation by means of Kuṇḍalinī. (Gorakṣaśataka 51)

Having joined the hands in the *sampuṭa* gesture and firmly assumed the *padmāsana* posture, placing the chin tightly against the chest and meditating upon that which is to be beheld, one should repeatedly exhale the filled *apāna* wind upward while releasing the *prāṇa*; through the awakening of the *śakti*, the person attains incomparable consciousness. (Gorakṣaśataka 52 = Haṭhayogapradīpikā 1.50)
One should perform massage of the limbs with water produced from physical exertion;
one should abandon pungent, sour, and salty foods, and practice a diet of milk. (GorS 2.53 = 1.50)
A practitioner of celibacy, moderate in diet, renounced, and devoted to yoga, shall become perfected after one year; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
When very unctuous and sweet food is eaten while omitting one-fourth of its quantity for the sake of pleasing the gods, that is called "moderate diet" (mitāhāra). (GorS 2.55 = HYP 1.60)
Above the *kanda* is the Kuṇḍalinī energy, coiled eightfold;
she is known as the binder of the deluded and the bestower of liberation upon yogins. (Gorakṣaśataka 56 = Haṭhayogapradīpikā 3.107)
The yogi who knows Mahāmudrā, the Namomudrā, Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, and the Mūlabandha, is a vessel for accomplishment. (GorS 2.57 = 1.32)
The purification of the network of channels, the movement of the moon and the sun, and the drying up of the bodily fluids—this is designated as Mahāmudrā. (Gorakṣaśataka 58)

Placing the chin upon the chest, pressing the vulva for a long time with the left foot, and likewise holding down the extended right foot with both hands, one should fill the two sides of the abdomen with breath and slowly exhale; this is declared to be the great *mudrā* that destroys the sins of men. (Gorakṣaśataka 59 = 1/33)
Having practiced with the lunar limb, one should practice again with the solar limb until the count becomes equal; thereafter, one should release the mudrā.
For neither wholesome nor unwholesome tastes are all devoid of flavor;
even terrible poison, once released, is digested like nectar.
Consumption, leprosy, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, indigestion, and other such ailments—his humors go to destruction if he practices Mahāmudrā. (GorS 2.62 = HYP 3.17)
This Mahāmudrā, which brings about great accomplishment for human beings, has been explained; it must be guarded with effort and should not be given to just anyone. (GorS 2.63 = HYP 3.18)
When the tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in reverse, and the gaze is directed between the eyebrows, this is the Khecarī Mudrā. (Gorakṣaśataka 64 = 1/34)
Neither disease, death, nor lassitude; neither sleep, hunger, nor thirst; nor even fainting shall befall him who knows the Khecarī Mudrā. (Gorakṣaśataka 65 = Haṭhayogapradīpikā 3.39)
He who knows the *khecarī* mudrā is not afflicted by disease, is not tainted by karma, and is not constrained by time. (Gorakṣaśataka 66 = Haṭhayogapradīpikā 3.40)
Since the mind moves in the void and the tongue has gone to move in the void,
this is therefore designated by the Siddhas as the mudrā named Khecarī.
The body has its root in the *bindu*, and the channels are established therein;
they nourish the body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
He by whom the aperture above the uvula is sealed by means of the Khecarī [mudrā],
his bindu does not leak, even when embraced by a passionate woman.
As long as the drop remains within the body, whence can there be fear of death?
As long as the sky-seal (nabho-mudrā) is bound, the drop does not depart. (GorS 70)
Even when the drop has moved and reached the fire,
it goes upward, drawn by Śakti and restrained by the Yoni-mudrā.
Furthermore, that drop (bindu) is of two kinds: white and likewise red;
they call the white semen, while the red is called mahārāja.
The *rajas* (passion), resembling liquid vermilion, is situated in the place of the sun;
the *bindu* (drop) is situated in the place of the moon. The unification of these two is very difficult to attain.
The *bindu* is Śiva, and the *rajas* is Śakti; the *bindu* is the moon and the *rajas* is the sun.
Only through the union of these two is the supreme state attained. (Gorakṣaśataka 74)
When the great *rajas*, impelled by the movement of power (*śakti*) through the vital wind (*vāyu*), attains oneness with the *bindu*, then the divine body arises. (Gorakṣaśataka 75)
Semen joined with the moon and the menstrual flow joined with the sun—
he who understands the unification of these two into a single, equal essence is a knower of Yoga.
Because that great bird flies without resting, that indeed is called Uḍḍīyāna; it is described as your bond.
In the western part of the abdomen, below the navel, this is declared to be the Uḍḍiyāna-bandha; there, the binding is performed.
For the network of vessels that flows downward binds the water of the head;
therefore, the Jālandhara-bandha is the destroyer of the flood of suffering in the throat. (Gorakṣaśataka 79 = Haṭhayogapradīpikā 3.71)
When the Jālandhara lock, characterized by the contraction of the throat, is performed,
the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the vital wind become provoked.
Pressing with the heel, one should contract the perineum and draw the *apāna* upward; this is called the *mūla-bandha*. (Gorakṣaśataka 81)
Through the unification of the apāna and prāṇa breaths, and by the depletion of urine and feces, even an old man becomes young through the constant practice of mūlabandha. (Gorakṣaśataka 82)

Having assumed the lotus posture with the body, head, and neck held straight, and with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, one should recite the imperishable syllable Oṃ in a secluded place. (GorS 2.83)
"Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ— these worlds, with Soma, Sūrya, and Agni as their deities,
abide within the measures of that which is the supreme light, Om."
The three times, the three Vedas, the three worlds, the three sovereigns,
and the three gods abide in that supreme light which is Om.
Action, will, and likewise knowledge—Brahmī, Raudrī, and Vaiṣṇavī—the triple power (śakti) which abides therein is the supreme light, Om. (GorS 2.86)
The letter A, the letter U, and the letter M known as the Bindu—
where these three morae (mātrās) reside, that is the supreme light, Om.
One should conquer that seed with speech, practice it fully with the body, and constantly remember it with the mind—that supreme light which is "Om. (Gorakṣaśataka 88)
Whether pure or impure, whoever constantly recites the *praṇava* is not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
When the breath moves, the drop moves; when it is still, the drop becomes still.
The yogi attains the state of a pillar; therefore, he should restrain the vital air. (Gorakṣaśataka 90)
As long as the vital breath remains in the body, so long is it said to be living;
death is its departure from there, therefore one should restrain the breath.
As long as the vital breath is bound within the body, as long as the mind is undisturbed,
and as long as the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, how can there be any fear of time?
Therefore, out of fear of time (death), Brahmā was devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma);
likewise, yogis and sages should restrain the vital air (vāyu). 93.
The *haṃsa* moves thirty-six finger-breadths outside through the left and right channels; therefore, it is called *prāṇa*. (GorS 2.94 = 1.40)
When the entire network of channels, which was previously clouded by impurities, becomes pure,
at that very moment the yogi becomes capable of mastering the vital breath.
The yogin, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana), should fill [the body] with breath through the moon;
having retained it according to his capacity, he should again exhale through the sun. (GorS 96 = 1/43)
Having meditated upon the orb of the moon as nectar, resembling curd and like silver-colored cow's milk, one who practices breath control shall become happy. (GorS 2.97 = 1.44)
Drawing in the breath through the right [nostril], one should slowly fill the abdomen;
having retained it according to the rule, one should exhale through the moon [the left nostril] as before.
Having meditated on the orb of the sun as a mass of blazing flames situated at the navel, the yogi shall become happy in the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). (GorS 2.99 = 1.46)

One should drink the breath in measured amounts through the iḍā and exhale it again through the other; having drunk the air through the piṅgalā, one should then hold it and release it through the vāmā.
For the self-controlled practitioner who meditates on the two orbs of the sun and the moon according to this method, the entire system of channels becomes purified after three months.
The retention of breath as desired, the kindling of the internal fire,
the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda), and the arising of health result from the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śodhana).
Thus ends the Gorakṣa-śataka.
